The Fulvous whistling duck (Dendrocygna bicolor) exhibits a remarkably rapid incubation period, with eggs hatching after 25 days [ab = 25 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a value that aligns with avibase records reporting a range of 24 to 26 days. Upon hatching, the precocial chicks display a wet weight at birth of 27.8 grams [Wwb = 27.8 grams], a relatively modest mass compared to other anatids of similar adult body size. This initial size is a critical determinant of early survival, as the downy young must begin exogenous feeding almost immediately. The initial wet weight of the egg itself, recorded at 51 grams [Ww0 = 51 grams], reflects the substantial investment of yolk and albumen required to sustain development over the incubation period. These measurements, gathered from captive breeding colonies, underscore the species' reliance on stable thermal conditions for successful embryogenesis.

Under the elevated body temperatures characteristic of active adults (41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]), a predictable sequence of developmental milestones governs the transition to independence. Fledging, the achievement of sustained flight, typically occurs 59 days after hatching [tx = 59 days after hatching], though field observations note a natural range of 55 to 63 days at a temperature of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]. This duration is shorter than that of larger-bodied congeners, likely reflecting an adaptive strategy to reduce nest vulnerability. Following fledging, the juvenile birds undergo a period of rapid somatic growth and feather maturation. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, is reached at 100 days after hatching [tp = 100 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime, a timing that allows individuals to complete the majority of their structural growth before reproductive allocation begins at a temperature of 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C].

The species exhibits a clear sexual size dimorphism in terms of ultimate mass. Adult females attain a maximum recorded body mass of 716.5 grams [Wwi = 716.5 grams], while their male counterparts are consistently heavier, reaching an asymptotic mass of 760.75 grams [Wwi = 760.75 grams]. This difference of approximately 44 grams is modest relative to some waterfowl but is consistent with the monogamous, biparental care system of the Dendrocygninae. The larger male mass may confer advantages in territory defense and competition for nesting sites. These adult masses are based on measurements from wild-caught individuals in Mexico and the southern United States, and they show relatively low inter-population variation. For comparative context, these values align closely with those reported for the closely related Dendrocygna autumnalis, though the fulvous species tends toward slightly larger average dimensions.

In terms of reproductive output, Fulvous whistling ducks are single-brooded, producing just one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. The clutch itself is substantial, ranging from 6 to 16 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 6 to 16 eggs per clutch], a broad range that reflects variation in female body condition, habitat quality, and latitude. This annual reproductive effort, when considered under the 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C] thermal conditions of the breeding season, represents a significant energetic investment. The first successful breeding event, which marks the initiation of reproductive life, occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when held at the same temperature. This one-year delay is common among migratory anatids and permits full skeletal development and the acquisition of foraging experience before the demanding tasks of nest building and incubation begin.

Longevity data for Dendrocygna bicolor, derived from both banding recoveries and captive records, indicate that the maximum lifespan reaches approximately 11.2 years [am = approximately 11.2 years] when evaluated under optimal captive conditions at 41.2 °C [T = 41.2 °C]. This figure translates to roughly 4,088 days and is consistent with the slow-paced life-history strategy typical of many medium-bodied waterfowl that invest heavily in a single annual brood. Wild birds likely experience reduced longevity due to predation pressure and environmental stochasticity. The combination of a single annual clutch, a modest clutch size, and a relatively extended lifespan creates a stable population dynamic. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as the product of clutch size and frequency, supports a relatively low but steady recruitment level. Data from long-term studies in Texas and Louisiana confirm that these ducks are capable of remarkable site fidelity, with some individuals returning to the same breeding marshes for over a decade.
